<STRUCT_0001>
Recall that a topological space <MATH_0001> is called <TEXTITOPEN_0001>catenary<TEXTITCLOSE_0001> if
for every pair of irreducible closed subsets <MATH_0002>
there exist a maximal chain of irreducible closed subsets
<MATH_0003>
and every such chain has the same length. See
Topology, Definition <REF_0001>.
Recall that a scheme is catenary if its underlying topological space
is catenary. See Properties, Definition <REF_0002>.

Let <MATH_0001> be a scheme. Assume <MATH_0002> is locally Noetherian.
We say <MATH_0003> is <TEXTITOPEN_0001>universally catenary<TEXTITCLOSE_0001> if for every
morphism <MATH_0004> locally of finite type the scheme <MATH_0005> is catenary.

<STRUCT_0001>
This is a ``better'' notion than catenary as there exist Noetherian schemes
which are catenary but not universally catenary. See
Examples, Section <REF_0001>.
Many schemes are universally catenary, see
Lemma <REF_0002> below.

<STRUCT_0002><STRUCT_0003>
Recall that a ring <MATH_0001> is called <TEXTITOPEN_0001>catenary<TEXTITCLOSE_0001> if
for any pair of prime ideals <MATH_0002>
there exists a maximal chain of primes
<MATH_0003>
and all of these have the same length. See
Algebra, Definition <REF_0003>.
We have seen the relationship between catenary schemes and
catenary rings in Properties, Section <REF_0004>.
Recall that a ring <MATH_0004> is called <TEXTITOPEN_0002>universally catenary<TEXTITCLOSE_0002> if
<MATH_0005> is Noetherian and for every finite type ring map <MATH_0006>
the ring <MATH_0007> is catenary. See
Algebra, Definition <REF_0005>.
Many interesting rings which come up
in algebraic geometry satisfy this property.
